issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident, 'Babies' as a salient auditory trigger is hard to connect clinically unless the accident specifically involved infants/crying, which is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger items (intrusive thoughts, nightmare residue) are generic trauma reactivation cues, making this item stand out as trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Make sure never to be alone with another person' suggests avoidance linked to fear of being accused of harming someone or of interpersonal/sexual threat, which is not coherently supported by the accident trauma type, threat items, or appraisals. The rest of the profile is organized around generalized danger/vulnerability, not being alone with another person specifically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after an accident, but here it lacks support from the other selected items. The threat and strategy items focus on physical danger and hypervigilance, while no memory or trigger content suggests shame-based social exposure. In this profile, humiliation is the least coherent appraisal and appears disconnected from the accident-focused formulation.

vignette:
Minh was thirty-three, a physical therapist at a suburban outpatient clinic, and he had been thriving—until the morning a year ago when a driver ran a red light and T-boned his sedan at sixty miles per hour. The impact crushed his pelvis, tore ligaments in his lower back, and left him trapped in the wreckage for forty-five minutes while the fuel line dripped. Surgery and months of rehabilitation followed, but Minh healed physically. What did not heal was what happened inside his mind.

Now, at work, a patient’s crutch clattering to the linoleum floor would send electricity through his spine—his heart slamming, his eyes darting to corners, searching for the source of danger as though a car were about to break through the wall. That split-second focus on threat was exhausting, yet he could not stop himself; the loud noise had already activated the hypervigilance that now governed his days. His concentration fractured: a colleague’s laugh could become a distant scream, and a spilled water bottle might as well be shattering glass. At night, he woke with dream residue—the screech of metal still ringing—and lay rigid, convinced that his body was fundamentally unreliable, that the healed fractures were a mask over permanent damage. Those intrusive thoughts and nightmare fragments also fed his sense that the world was full of hidden dangers: you could never know who would harm you, or where the next lethal blow would come from.

That conviction—that his body could not be trusted and that others were unpredictable threats—spawned a set of rituals. Minh began mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios before every interaction: picturing a patient collapsing on the treatment table, a fire alarm going off mid-session, a stranger walking in with hostile intent. He also cleaned and organised his treatment room repeatedly—aligning the weights, stacking the Therabands, polishing the counter—because the order made him feel, fleetingly, in control. At home, he found himself checking the sharp edges of kitchen knives, noticing the heavy lamp that could be used as a weapon, though he never told his wife why. These strategies, however, backfired: scanning the environment for signs of threat only sharpened his vigilance, so that a shadow moving in the hallway would trigger another startle response, another wave of fear that something terrible was about to happen. The more he checked, the more dangers he saw—a loop that tightened around his every conscious moment.

His wife began to notice. He would come home from work hollow-eyed, and when she asked about his day he said little, because explaining that he had spent hours replaying the worst possible outcomes for a routine ankle sprain seemed absurd. She saw him lock the front door three times before bed, then check the windows. She asked what he was afraid of, and Minh could only say, “Anyone could come in. I don’t know.” The fear of harm had graduated from a thought to a constant state; it made him avoid crowds, avoid driving past the intersection where the accident happened, avoid letting his wife drive alone because he could not stop imagining the wreckage. At work, he became known as the meticulous therapist, but his colleagues did not know that the compulsion to tidy was a fragile dam against panic.

What brought him to therapy, finally, was a morning when a patient’s grandson slammed a door in the waiting room. Minh’s body went cold; he dropped the goniometer, excused himself, and locked himself in the supply closet for fifteen minutes, chest heaving. He could not keep doing this—could not keep living as though the crash were still happening, as though his own flesh were made of glass. He wanted to believe the world was not that dangerous, that his body was not that fragile. He hoped, though he doubted it was possible, that someone could show him how to stop the rehearsing, the cleaning, the watching. He sat in the intake chair with his hands clasped, and said, “I don’t know how to be normal anymore.”
